claim: The nuclear RNA exosome complex mediates the processing of structured RNAs and the decay of aberrant non-coding RNAs, an important function particularly in human cells.
source: The nuclear RNA exosome complex mediates the processing of structured RNAs and the decay of aberrant non-coding RNAs, an important function particularly in human cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about exosome function presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The human exosome embeds a longer RNA channel than its yeast counterpart in biochemical assays.
source: In biochemical assays, the human exosome embeds a longer RNA channel than its yeast counterpart.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNase protection assays shown in Figure 1B comparing yeast and human complexes.

claim: The 3.8 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the core complex bound to a single-stranded RNA reveals that the RNA channel path is formed by two distinct features of the hDIS3 exoribonuclease: an open conformation and a domain organization more similar to bacterial RNase II than to yeast Rrp44.
source: The 3.8 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the core complex bound to a single-stranded RNA reveals that the RNA channel path is formed by two distinct features of the hDIS3 exoribonuclease: an open conformation and a domain organization more similar to bacterial RNase II than to yeast Rrp44.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure determination and structural comparisons shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the holo-complex shows how obligate nuclear cofactors position the hMTR4 helicase at the entrance of the core complex, suggesting a striking structural conservation from lower to higher eukaryotes.
source: The cryo-EM structure of the holo-complex shows how obligate nuclear cofactors position the hMTR4 helicase at the entrance of the core complex, suggesting a striking structural conservation from lower to higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure of hEXO-14 shown in Figure 7 and comparison with yeast structures.

claim: The exosome was originally discovered in S. cerevisiae as a complex of ribosomal RNA processing (Rrp) factors.
source: Indeed, the exosome was originally discovered in S. cerevisiae as a complex of ribosomal RNA processing (Rrp) factors (Mitchell et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 1997.

claim: The yeast exosome has a human counterpart in the so-called PM-Scl complex, which had been identified as the target of autoantibodies in patients suffering from polymyositis-scleroderma overlap syndrome (PM-Scl).
source: Soon afterwards, it became apparent that the yeast exosome has a human counterpart in the so-called PM-Scl complex, which had been identified as the target of autoantibodies in patients suffering from polymyositis-scleroderma overlap syndrome (PM-Scl) (Allmang et al., 1999b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allmang et al., 1999b.

claim: Several Mendelian diseases are now known to be associated with mutations in subunits of the human exosome complex.
source: Several Mendelian diseases are now known to be associated with mutations in subunits of the human exosome complex (reviewed in Morton et al., 2018; Reis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Both the yeast and human exosomes are centered around a scaffold of nine catalytically inactive subunits forming a barrel-like structure, with a ring of six 'base' proteins and a ring of three 'cap' proteins.
source: Both the yeast and human exosomes are centered around a scaffold of nine catalytically inactive subunits forming a barrel-like structure, with a ring of six 'base' proteins and a ring of three 'cap' proteins (Dziembowski et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2006; Makino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The essential catalytic activity of the S. cerevisiae complex is contributed by the tenth subunit, an RNase II-like 3'−5' exoribonuclease known as Rrp44 or Dis3.
source: The essential catalytic activity of the S. cerevisiae complex is contributed by the tenth subunit, an RNase II-like 3'−5' exoribonuclease known as Rrp44 or Dis3 (Dziembowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dziembowski et al., 2007.

claim: Yeast Rrp44 is tethered to the base of the exosome barrel to form yExo-10, the processive ribonuclease core common to the nuclear and cytoplasmic yeast exosome complexes.
source: Yeast Rrp44 (yRrp44) is tethered to the base of the exosome barrel to form yExo-10 (Bonneau et al., 2009; Makino et al., 2013), the processive ribonuclease core common to the nuclear and cytoplasmic yeast exosome complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: A long RNA-binding channel spans yExo-10, starting with a narrow entry pore in the cap ring, continuing in the central cavity of the base ring and ending at the yRrp44 exoribonuclease site.
source: A long RNA-binding channel spans yExo-10, starting with a narrow entry pore in the cap ring, continuing in the central cavity of the base ring and ending at the yRrp44 exoribonuclease site (Bonneau et al., 2009; Makino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The 9-subunit barrel associates with two distinct yRrp44 orthologues, hDIS3 and hDIS3L, to form nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic hEXO-10 complexes, respectively.
source: Proteomic studies of human exosome complexes recently showed that the 9-subunit barrel associates with two distinct yRrp44 orthologues, hDIS3 and hDIS3L, to form nucleoplasmic and cytoplasmic hEXO-10 complexes, respectively (Staals et al., 2010; Tomecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to proteomic studies.

claim: The third paralogue of yRrp44, the cytoplasmic protein hDIS3L2, functions independently of the RNA exosome.
source: The third paralogue of yRrp44, the cytoplasmic protein hDIS3L2, instead functions independently of the RNA exosome (Chang et al., 2013; Lubas et al., 2013; Malecki et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in hDIS3 but not hDIS3L have been identified in patients with multiple myeloma.
source: Intriguingly, mutations in hDIS3 but not hDIS3L have been identified in patients with multiple myeloma (Chapman et al., 2011; Lionetti et al., 2015; Tomecki et al., 2014), underscoring the importance of the nuclear form of the complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: In yeast, the yRrp6 exoribonuclease and its binding partner yRrp47 are tethered with high affinity to the cap of yExo-9 and target the complex to the nuclear compartment.
source: In yeast, the yRrp6 exoribonuclease and its binding partner yRrp47 are tethered with high affinity to the cap of yExo-9 (Kowalinski et al., 2016; Makino et al., 2015; Zinder et al., 2016) and target the complex to the nuclear compartment (Gonzales-Zubiate et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The yRrp6-yRrp47 dimer together with another stably associated subunit, yMpp6, recruits the essential 3'−5' RNA helicase yMtr4.
source: The yRrp6-yRrp47 dimer together with another stably associated subunit, yMpp6, recruits the essential 3'−5' RNA helicase yMtr4 (Falk et al., 2017; Schuch et al., 2014; Wasmuth et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In a recent cryo-EM structure of the yeast 14-subunit nuclear exosome bound to a pre-60S ribosomal particle, the physiological RNA substrate (a 5.8S pre-ribosomal RNA precursor) was observed being channeled from yMtr4 into the exosome core.
source: Indeed, in a recent cryo-EM structure of the yeast 14-subunit nuclear exosome bound to a pre-60S ribosomal particle, we could observe the physiological RNA substrate (a 5.8S pre-ribosomal RNA precursor) being channeled from yMtr4 into the exosome core (Schuller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous cryo-EM study by the authors.

claim: Orthologues of nuclear exosome cofactors have been identified in human cells: EXOSC10 (hRRP6), C1D (hRRP47), MPH6 (hMPP6) and MTREX (hMTR4).
source: Orthologues of these nuclear exosome cofactors have been identified in human cells: EXOSC10 (hRRP6), C1D (hRRP47), MPH6 (hMPP6) and MTREX (hMTR4) (Schilders et al., 2007a; 2005; Schilders et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The processing of the 5.8S rRNA is a common role of nucleoplasmic exosome complexes, with similar intermediates being formed in yeast and human cells.
source: The processing of the 5.8S rRNA is a common role of nucleoplasmic exosome complexes, with similar intermediates being formed in yeast and human cells (Allmang et al., 1999a; Briggs et al., 1998; Tafforeau et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Degradation of the 5' ETS, a byproduct of ribosome biogenesis, is a function of both yeast and human nucleolar exosome complexes, but different cofactors are involved.
source: Degradation of the 5' ETS, a byproduct of ribosome biogenesis, is also a function of both yeast and human nucleolar exosome complexes, but different cofactors are involved (Sudo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The major function of the human nuclear exosome appears to lie in quality control pathways that counteract pervasive transcription initiation and defective transcription termination.
source: The major function of the human nuclear exosome, however, appears to lie in quality control pathways that counteract pervasive transcription initiation and defective transcription termination (Belair et al., 2018; Ogami et al., 2018; Szczepińska et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nucleoplasmic exosome targets promoter upstream transcripts (PROMPTs) that arise due to antisense transcription from bidirectional promoters.
source: For example, the nucleoplasmic exosome targets promoter upstream transcripts (PROMPTs) that arise due to antisense transcription from bidirectional promoters (Preker et al., 2008) and prematurely terminated products of protein coding genes (Szczepińska et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human cells have evolved specialized cofactor complexes built around hMTR4.
source: In line with the prevalence of these pathways, human cells have evolved specialized cofactor complexes built around hMTR4 (Lubas et al., 2011; Meola et al., 2016; Ogami et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast yExo-10cat showed a bimodal protection pattern in RNase A/T1 assays, with the accumulation of 31–33 and 11–12 nucleotide fragments.
source: As we had previously reported (Bonneau et al., 2009), yeast yExo-10cat showed a bimodal protection pattern in RNase A/T1 assays, with the accumulation of 31–33 and 11–12 nucleotide fragments (Figure 1B, lane 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: The long 31–33 nucleotide fragments correspond to the channel path, whereby RNA traverses the central channel of yExo-9 to reach the exoribonuclease site of yRrp44.
source: The long 31–33 nucleotide fragments correspond to the so-called channel path, whereby RNA traverses the central channel of yExo-9 to reach the exoribonuclease site of yRrp44 (Makino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: The channel path is used by the majority of RNAs in yeast.
source: This path is used by the majority of RNAs in yeast (Drazkowska et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2012; Wasmuth and Lima, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The short 11–12 nucleotide fragments are thought to reflect the presence of an alternative direct path to the exoribonuclease site that is used in vivo by a limited number of nuclear RNAs.
source: The short 11–12 nucleotide fragments are thought to reflect the presence of an alternative direct path to the exoribonuclease site that is used in vivo by a limited number of nuclear RNAs (Han and van Hoof, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The two RNA paths have been visualized structurally, and correlate with two different conformations of the yRrp44 ribonuclease: a closed conformation for the long channel path and an open conformation for the short direct path.
source: The two RNA paths have been visualized structurally, and correlate with two different conformations of the yRrp44 ribonuclease: a closed conformation for the long channel path and an open conformation for the short direct path (Makino et al., 2015, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Human hEXO-10cat treatment with RNase A/T1 resulted in a bimodal distribution with the accumulation of short fragments (11–12 nucleotides) and long fragments (~34–37 nucleotides), but the latter were much less abundant as compared to yExo-10cat.
source: In the case of human hEXO-10cat, treatment with RNase A/T1 also resulted in a bimodal distribution with the accumulation of short fragments (11–12 nucleotides) and long fragments (~34–37 nucleotides), but the latter were much less abundant as compared to yExo-10cat (Figure 1B, lane 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Benzonase treatment resulted in a unimodal protection pattern for both the yeast and the human complexes, with only the long fragments accumulating.
source: Benzonase treatment resulted in a unimodal protection pattern for both the yeast and the human complexes, with only the long fragments accumulating (Figure 1B, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The long fragments accumulating upon benzonase treatment spanned 35–39 nucleotides for yeast yExo-10cat and 39–43 nucleotides for human hEXO-10cat.
source: The long fragments accumulating upon benzonase treatment spanned 35–39 nucleotides for yeast yExo-10cat and 39–43 nucleotides for human hEXO-10cat (Figure 1B, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The human nuclear exosome core is likely to thread RNA through the central channel, but the path is more extended than in the yeast complex.
source: We concluded that the human nuclear exosome core is likely to thread RNA through the central channel, but the path is more extended than in the yeast complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNase protection assay data.

claim: The size of the protected RNA fragments increases by about 10–15 nucleotides when yExo10cat is incubated with its nuclear cofactors, including a catalytically inactive version of yRrp6, yRrp47, yMpp6 and yMtr4 in the presence of ADP.
source: In case of the yeast proteins, we have previously shown biochemically that the size of the protected RNA fragments increases of about 10–15 nucleotides when yExo10cat is incubated with its nuclear cofactors, including a catalytically inactive version of yRrp6 (yRrp6cat Asp296Asn), yRrp47, yMpp6 and yMtr4 in the presence of ADP (Falk et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The footprint of yeast nuclear exosome reflects the channeling of RNA from yMtr4 into the exosome core.
source: Structural studies have shown that this footprint reflects the channeling of RNA from yMtr4 into the exosome core (Schuller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study by the authors.

claim: The covalently linked hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 complex behaved as wild-type hEXO-10cat in RNase protection assays.
source: The covalently linked hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 complex behaved as wild-type hEXO-10cat (Figure 1C, compare lane 1 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When incubating hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 with hRRP6cat-hRRP47 and hMTR4 in the presence of ADP, a shift to longer fragments was observed.
source: When incubating hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 with hRRP6cat-hRRP47 and hMTR4 in the presence of ADP, we observed a shift to longer fragments (Figure 1C, lane 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The presence of all four cofactors and ADP was required to have a stronger shift to ~50 nucleotides in the human exosome.
source: The presence of all four cofactors and ADP was required to have a stronger shift to ~50 nucleotides (lane 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Mtr4-exosome needs at least one cofactor to be stabilized and all of them to show strong association, both in the yeast and human system.
source: Thus, it appears that the Mtr4-exosome needs at least one cofactor to be stabilized and all of them to show strong association, both in the yeast and human system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNase protection assay data.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure of yeast nuclear yExo-14 with a pre-60S substrate, channeling through yMtr4 requires a large conformational change of yRrp6-yRrp47.
source: In the cryo-EM structure of yeast nuclear yExo-14 with a pre-60S substrate (Schuller et al., 2018), we had observed that channeling through yMtr4 requires a large conformational change of yRrp6-yRrp47 (Makino et al., 2015): the ribonuclease domain of yRrp6 was displaced from the top of yExo-9 (to allow binding of the yMtr4 helicase on the yRrp4 cap protein) and the N-terminal hetero-dimerization module (yRrp6N-yRrp47) was displaced from the yRrp6 ribonuclease domain (and instead bound yMtr4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous cryo-EM study by the authors.

claim: Channeling through the helicase does not require (and may actually be competing with) the ribonuclease domain of yRrp6.
source: The prediction from this observation is that channeling through the helicase does not require (and may actually be competing with) the ribonuclease domain of yRrp6.
evidence: This is a prediction/inference drawn from the structural observation.

claim: Using covalently linked hRRP6N instead of full-length hRRP6 appeared to stabilize the 50 nucleotide fragments in RNase protection assays.
source: Using covalently linked hRRP6N instead of f.l. hRRP6 appeared to even stabilize the 50 nucleotide fragments (compare lanes 8 and 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The most likely reason for the stabilization of 50 nucleotide fragments is the improved biochemical properties and stability of hRRP6N as compared to the full-length protein.
source: The most likely reason for this stabilization is the improved biochemical properties and stability of hRRP6N as compared to the full-length protein, allowing us to overcome the hRRP6 stoichiometry issues in the reconstituted complexes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: A similar increase in the size of the protected fragments was observed in both the yeast and human systems when comparing the 10-subunit core complexes with the 14-subunit nuclear holo-complexes.
source: When comparing the 10-subunit core complexes with the 14-subunit nuclear holo-complexes, we observed a similar increase in the size of the protected fragments in both the yeast and human systems (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The human hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 cryo-EM structure was obtained at 3.80 Å resolution.
source: From the larger particle population we obtained the structure of human hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 at 3.80 Å resolution and from a smaller one we obtained the structure of hEXO-14cat at 6.25 Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM data processing results.

claim: The structure of hEXO-14cat was obtained at 6.25 Å resolution.
source: From the larger particle population we obtained the structure of human hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 at 3.80 Å resolution and from a smaller one we obtained the structure of hEXO-14cat at 6.25 Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM data processing results.

claim: The excellent quality of the cryo-EM density allowed significant improvement of the stereochemistry of the hEXO-9 atomic model, which now has less than 1% Ramachandran and rotamer outliers.
source: The excellent quality of the cryo-EM density allowed us to significantly improve the stereochemistry of the hEXO-9 atomic model, which now has less than 1% Ramachandran and rotamer outliers (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model refinement statistics in Table 1.

claim: The resulting structure of hEXO-9 has the characteristic base ring of adjacent hRRP41-hRRP42-hMTR3-hRRP43-hRRP46-hRRP45 subunits and the cap ring of adjacent hRRP4-hCSL4-hRRP40 subunits first observed by X-ray crystallography.
source: The resulting structure of hEXO-9 has the characteristic base ring of adjacent hRRP41-hRRP42-hMTR3-hRRP43-hRRP46-hRRP45 subunits and the cap ring of adjacent hRRP4-hCSL4-hRRP40 subunits first observed by X-ray crystallography (Liu et al., 2006) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure and citation to previous crystallography work.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure, hCSL4 is only partially ordered.
source: In the cryo-EM structure, hCSL4 is only partially ordered.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Similar observations of partial ordering have been made in a previous cryo-EM structure of yeast yExo-10, as yCsl4 is known to be stabilized by the C-terminal region of yRrp6.
source: Similar observations have been made in a previous cryo-EM structure of yeast yExo-10 (Wang et al., 2007), as yCsl4 is known to be stabilized by the C-terminal region of yRrp6 (Makino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure, the C-terminal tail of hRRP45 (after residue 278) does not wrap around other subunits of the base but instead residues 280–287 bend backwards to form a β-strand, completing the hRRP45 β-sheet.
source: First, in the cryo-EM structure the C-terminal tail of hRRP45 (after residue 278) does not wrap around other subunits of the base. Instead, residues 280–287 bend backwards to form a β-strand, completing the hRRP45 β-sheet (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-terminus of hMTR3 is well ordered in the cryo-EM structure: it aligns on the hRRP43 β-sheet and then continues in the internal channel of hEXO-9.
source: Second, the N-terminus of hMTR3 is well ordered as compared to the hEXO-9 crystal structure: it aligns on the hRRP43 β-sheet and then continues in the internal channel of hEXO-9 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A similar arrangement of the N-terminus of Mtr3 was previously observed in the yeast yMtr3 orthologue.
source: A similar arrangement was previously observed in the yeast yMtr3 orthologue (Kowalinski et al., 2016; Makino et al., 2015; 2013; Zinder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The N-terminus of hRRP4 is well ordered in the cryo-EM density and packs against the hRRP42 β-sheet.
source: The N-terminus of hRRP4 is also well ordered in the cryo-EM density and packs against the hRRP42 β-sheet (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: An analogous interaction of the N-terminus of Rrp4 has been observed for yeast yRrp4.
source: An analogous interaction has been observed for yeast yRrp4 (Kowalinski et al., 2016; Makino et al., 2015, 2013; Zinder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The yeast and human barrels are even more similar than previously thought.
source: Thus, the yeast and human barrels are even more similar than previously thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural comparisons.

claim: The cryo-EM reconstruction showed density at the top of hRRP40 at the same position where yeast yMpp6 binds yExo-9.
source: As a note, the cryo-EM reconstruction also showed density at the top of hRRP40 at the same position where yeast yMpp6 binds yExo-9 (Falk et al., 2017; Schuller et al., 2018; Wasmuth et al., 2017) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous studies.

claim: In comparison to the yeast structure, the cryo-EM density of the human complex shows an additional structural feature of hMPP6, an α-helix that interacts intra-molecularly with an extended segment of hMPP6.
source: In comparison to the yeast structure, the cryo-EM density of the human complex shows an additional structural feature of hMPP6, an α-helix that interacts intra-molecularly with an extended segment of hMPP6 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3E.

claim: While the other cofactors of the nuclear exosome detached from the core in this particle population, the hMPP6 interaction with the core complex remained.
source: We conclude that while the other cofactors of the nuclear exosome detached from the core in this particle population, the hMPP6 interaction with the core complex remained.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: hDIS3 has a similar domain organization as yeast yRrp44, with a PIN-domain region followed by an exoribonuclease region typical of the RNase II family of proteins.
source: hDIS3 has a similar domain organization as yeast yRrp44, with a PIN-domain region followed by an exoribonuclease region typical of the RNase II family of proteins (Tomecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and structural comparison.

claim: The CR3 motif of hDIS3 forms a long β-hairpin wedged between hRRP41-hRRP42, similarly to the yeast exosome structure.
source: Similarly to the yeast exosome structure (Makino et al., 2013), the corresponding CR3 motif of hDIS3 forms a long β-hairpin wedged between hRRP41-hRRP42 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4A and citation to previous work.

claim: The CR3 motif of hDIS3 is twenty-residue shorter and lacks a yRrp41-interacting loop corresponding to yRrp44 residues 60–67.
source: However, the CR3 motif of hDIS3 is twenty-residue shorter and lacks a yRrp41-interacting loop (corresponding to yRrp44 residues 60–67, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The human complex lacks the interaction between the core and the exoribonuclease that was observed in the yeast exosome, namely the contact between yRrp44 and the C-terminus of yRrp45.
source: Furthermore, the human complex lacks another interaction between the core and the exoribonuclease that was observed in the yeast exosome, namely the contact between yRrp44 and the C-terminus of yRrp45 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4B.

claim: While yeast yRrp44 can stably interact with the yRrp41-yRrp45 heterodimer, the interaction between the human orthologues is weaker.
source: Consistently, while yeast yRrp44 can stably interact with the yRrp41-yRrp45 heterodimer (Bonneau et al., 2009), size-exclusion chromatography experiments with recombinant proteins showed that the interaction between the human orthologues is weaker (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 4C and citation to previous work.

claim: The exoribonuclease region of hDIS3 includes two N-terminal cold-shock domains (CSD1 and CSD2), a catalytic domain (RNB) and a C-terminal S1 domain.
source: The exoribonuclease region includes two N-terminal cold-shock domains (CSD1 and CSD2), a catalytic domain (RNB) and a C-terminal S1 domain (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: The three OB folds are positioned on top of the RNB domain, with CSD1 and CSD2 forming a lobe on one side of the RNB domain and facing the S1 domain on the other side.
source: The three OB folds are positioned on top of the RNB domain, with CSD1 and CSD2 forming a lobe on one side of the RNB domain and facing the S1 domain on the other side (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5.

claim: A similar overall arrangement of OB folds has been described for all other known members of the RNase II protein family.
source: A similar overall arrangement has been described for all other known members of this protein family (Frazão et al., 2006; Lorentzen et al., 2008) (Faehnle et al., 2014) (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In hDIS3, the CSD lobe is separated from the S1 lobe by a large funnel-like cleft, reminiscent of OB fold arrangement present in RNase II and DIS3L2.
source: In hDIS3, the CSD lobe is separated from the S1 lobe by a large funnel-like cleft, reminiscent of OB fold arrangement present in RNase II and DIS3L2 (Faehnle et al., 2014; Frazão et al., 2006) (Figure 5A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5 and citations to previous studies.

claim: In yeast yRrp44 a rotation of the CSD lobe towards the S1 domain narrows the cleft.
source: In contrast, in yeast yRrp44 a rotation of the CSD lobe towards the S1 domain narrows the cleft (Lorentzen et al., 2008; Makino et al., 2015) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies and comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Two structural features of CSD1 specific to the yeast protein occlude and seal the narrow cleft (an extended segment at yRrp44 residues 327–347 and a helix at residues 366–384).
source: Furthermore, two structural features of CSD1 specific to the yeast protein occlude and seal the narrow cleft (an extended segment at yRrp44 residues 327–347 and a helix at residues 366–384) (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5B,E.

claim: yRrp44 does not feature an apical opening between the OB-fold domains.
source: As a result, yRrp44 does not feature an apical opening between the OB-fold domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural features.

claim: The rotation of the CSD lobe in yRrp44 creates a lateral opening for the RNA, between the CSD1 and RNB domains.
source: Instead, the rotation of the CSD lobe creates a lateral opening for the RNA, between the CSD1 and RNB domains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In yeast Rrp44, RNA enters the catalytic chamber of the RNB domain from the lateral opening between the CSD1 and RNB domains.
source: In previous crystal structures of the RNase II family members, the position of the OB folds has been shown to shape the path with which RNA enters the catalytic chamber of the RNB domain: in yeast Rrp44, RNA enters the catalytic chamber of the RNB domain from the lateral opening between the CSD1 and RNB domains (Lorentzen et al., 2008) while in RNase II and DIS3L2, RNA enters from the apical opening between the CSD lobe and the S1 domain (Faehnle et al., 2014; Frazão et al., 2006) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In RNase II and DIS3L2, RNA enters the catalytic chamber from the apical opening between the CSD lobe and the S1 domain.
source: In previous crystal structures of the RNase II family members, the position of the OB folds has been shown to shape the path with which RNA enters the catalytic chamber of the RNB domain: in yeast Rrp44, RNA enters the catalytic chamber of the RNB domain from the lateral opening between the CSD1 and RNB domains (Lorentzen et al., 2008) while in RNase II and DIS3L2, RNA enters from the apical opening between the CSD lobe and the S1 domain (Faehnle et al., 2014; Frazão et al., 2006) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The RNA-binding path in hDIS3 is determined by the position of the OB folds.
source: As described below, the RNA-binding path in hDIS3 is also determined by the position of the OB folds (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis.

claim: The overall position of the hDIS3 exoribonuclease region on hEXO-9 does not resemble the closed conformation with which yeast yRrp44 binds RNAs entering from the long channel path but rather the open conformation with which yeast Rrp44 binds RNA in the direct access path.
source: In the cryo-EM structure, the overall position of the hDIS3 exoribonuclease region on hEXO-9 (Figure 6A) does not resemble the closed conformation with which yeast yRrp44 binds RNAs entering from the long channel path (Makino et al., 2013) (Figure 6B) but rather the open conformation with which yeast Rrp44 binds RNA in the direct access path (Makino et al., 2015) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6 and citations to previous studies.

claim: The PIN region and exoribonuclease region of hDIS3 are even less connected than observed in the open conformation of yeast yRrp44, with a large solvent channel between them.
source: The PIN region and exoribonuclease region of hDIS3 are even less connected than observed in the open conformation of yeast yRrp44, with a large solvent channel between them (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: A tube of density corresponding to a long single-stranded RNA bound in the channel path of hEXO-10 was observed in the reconstructed 3D volume.
source: When inspecting the reconstructed 3D volume for un-modeled density features, we could observe a tube of density corresponding to a long single-stranded RNA bound in the channel path of hEXO-10 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The ribonucleotide chain binds a positively-charged surface of hRRP4 and is threaded from the cap ring into the internal chamber of hEXO-9.
source: The ribonucleotide chain binds a positively-charged surface of hRRP4 and is threaded from the cap ring into the internal chamber of hEXO-9.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The RNA approaches the N-terminus of hMTR3 and proceeds by binding between hRRP41 and hRRP45, at the same binding path that is conserved not only in the yeast exosome but even in archaeal exosome-like complexes.
source: Here, the RNA approaches the N-terminus of hMTR3 and proceeds by binding between hRRP41 and hRRP45, at the same binding path that is conserved not only in the yeast exosome (Bonneau et al., 2009; Makino et al., 2013) but even in archaeal exosome-like complexes (Lorentzen and Conti, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure and citations to previous studies.

claim: After exiting from hEXO-9, the ribonucleotide chain continues directly into hDIS3, first binding in a surface groove formed by the juxtaposition of the PIN and CSD2 domains.
source: After exiting from hEXO-9, the ribonucleotide chain continues directly into hDIS3. First, it binds in a surface groove formed by the juxtaposition of the PIN and CSD2 domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The PIN domain engages a lateral surface to shape the RNA-binding cleft, while the adjacent front surface (which contains the predicted endoribonuclease site) is exposed to solvent.
source: The PIN domain engages a lateral surface to shape the RNA-binding cleft, while the adjacent front surface (which contains the predicted endoribonuclease site [Lebreton et al., 2008; Schaeffer et al., 2009; Schneider et al., 2009; Tomecki et al., 2010]) is exposed to solvent (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous studies.

claim: The ribonucleotide chain flanks the CSD lobe and traverses the wide solvent-exposed channel that separates the PIN and exoribonuclease regions.
source: The ribonucleotide chain then flanks the CSD lobe and traverses the wide solvent-exposed channel that separates the PIN and exoribonuclease regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The RNA continues in the funnel-like cleft between CSD1 and S1 domains and finally enters the RNB domain to reach the exoribonuclease active site.
source: The RNA continues in the funnel-like cleft between CSD1 and S1 domains and finally enters the RNB domain to reach the exoribonuclease active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The RNA-binding residues in the RNB domain are conserved in all members of the RNase II protein family.
source: The RNA-binding residues in the RNB domain (Figure 6D) are conserved in all members of this protein family.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6D and knowledge of protein family conservation.

claim: The entrance into the RNB domain from the apical CSD1-S1 route in hDIS3 is similar to bacterial RNase II and to DIS3L2 and differs from the lateral CSD1-RNB route of yeast Rrp44.
source: The entrance into the RNB domain from the apical CSD1-S1 route is similar to bacterial RNase II and to DIS3L2 and differs from the lateral CSD1-RNB route of yeast Rrp44, consistently with the structural organization of their OB-fold domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The long RNA channel path in the human exosome is formed by the combination of an open conformation of hDIS3 and an apical entry to the exoribonuclease active site.
source: The long RNA channel path in the human exosome is thus formed by the combination of an open conformation of hDIS3 and an apical entry to the exoribonuclease active site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: The long RNA channel path in the yeast exosome is formed by a closed conformation of yRrp44 and a lateral entry to the exoribonuclease active site.
source: In contrast, the long RNA channel path in the yeast exosome is formed by a closed conformation of yRrp44 and a lateral entry to the exoribonuclease active site (Bonneau et al., 2009; Makino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In the yeast complex, the open conformation of yRrp44 is not compatible with the formation of the long RNA channel path, as a possible access to the lateral entry of Rrp44 is sterically blocked by structural features of yeast exosome subunits (yRrp43 residues 100–120).
source: In the yeast complex, the open conformation of yRrp44 is not compatible with the formation of the long RNA channel path, as a possible access to the lateral entry of Rrp44 is sterically blocked by structural features of yeast exosome subunits (yRrp43 residues 100–120, [Zinder et al., 2016]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The RNA channel path in the structure of the human exosome core is longer as compared to that in the S. cerevisiae complex, explaining the longer footprint in the RNase protection assays.
source: The features we observed in the cryo-EM reconstruction rationalize the differences between the human and yeast core complexes that we had observed in the biochemical assays (Figure 1). First, the RNA channel path in the structure of the human exosome core is longer as compared to that in the S. cerevisiae complex (Makino et al., 2013), explaining the longer footprint in the RNase protection assays (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion that integrates structural and biochemical data.

claim: The segment of RNA connecting hEXO-9 and hDIS3 is more exposed to solvent than in the closed conformation of the yeast complex, explaining the increased sensitivity to small RNases in the protection experiment.
source: Second, the segment of RNA connecting hEXO-9 and hDIS3is is more exposed to solvent than in the closed conformation of the yeast complex, explaining the increased sensitivity to small RNases in the protection experiment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion that integrates structural and biochemical data.

claim: The atomic model built in the cryo-EM structure of hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 could be fitted without modifications in the density of hEXO-14cat, which featured the same open conformation of hDIS3.
source: The atomic model we had built in the cryo-EM structure of hEXO-10cat-hMPP6 could be fitted without modifications in the density of hEXO-14cat, which featured the same open conformation of hDIS3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis of hEXO-14cat.

claim: The nuclear cofactors in hEXO-14cat could be identified based on their distinct structural features and knowledge from the cryo-EM reconstruction of a yeast nuclear exosome complex.
source: Although the resolution we achieved for this particle population was lower than for the exosome core, we could identify the nuclear cofactors based on their distinct structural features and knowledge from the cryo-EM reconstruction of a yeast nuclear exosome complex (Schuller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: The atomic coordinates of yMtr4-yRrp6N-yRrp47 could be fitted in the equivalent position on the human exosome core.
source: Indeed, we could fit the atomic coordinates of yMtr4-yRrp6N-yRrp47 in the equivalent position on the human exosome core (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Density corresponding to the DExH core of hMTR4 is present on the top of hEXO-9, binding a similar surface of the cap protein hRRP4 and in a similar edge-on conformation as observed in yeast yExo-14.
source: In the hEXO14cat reconstruction, density corresponding to the DExH core of hMTR4 is present on the top of hEXO-9, binding a similar surface of the cap protein hRRP4 and in a similar edge-on conformation as observed in yeast yExo-14 (Schuller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure and citation to previous work.

claim: In the reconstruction of hEXO14cat, the KOW domain is more flexible, but ordered density is present for the stalk and the hRRP6N-hRRP47 heterodimer.
source: In the reconstruction of hEXO14cat, the KOW domain is more flexible, but ordered density is present for the stalk and the hRRP6N-hRRP47 heterodimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A small density feature was observed at the same position on the DExH core where the binding of the N-terminal segment of yMpp6 had been previously mapped.
source: Careful inspection of the reconstruction corresponding to hMTR4-hRRP6N-hRRP47 revealed a small density feature at the same position on the DExH core where we had previously mapped the binding of the N-terminal segment of yMpp6 (Schuller et al., 2018) (Figure 7A, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 7A and citation to previous work.

claim: The recruitment and edge-on conformation of the nuclear helicase over the entrance of the exosome core does not appear to be a specialized feature of the yeast exosome when bound to the pre-60S substrate, but rather an evolutionary conserved assembly of the nuclear exosome cofactors.
source: Thus, the recruitment and edge-on conformation of the nuclear helicase over the entrance of the exosome core does not appear to be a specialized feature of the yeast exosome when bound to the pre-60S substrate, but rather an evolutionary conserved assembly of the nuclear exosome cofactors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural comparison between human and yeast complexes.

claim: A conserved positively-charged surface on the yMtr4 DExH core approaches a conserved negatively-charged surface of yRrp6N in the cryo-EM structure of yeast yExo-14.
source: When examining the interaction between yRrp6N-yRrp47 and yMtr4 in the cryo-EM structure of yeast yExo-14, we had previously noted that a conserved positively-charged surface on the yMtr4 DExH core approaches a conserved negatively-charged surface of yRrp6N (Schuller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous structural work by the authors.

claim: Arg887, Arg890 and Arg891 of yMtr4 point towards Asp86, Glu90, and Asp96 of yRrp6.
source: Specifically, Arg887, Arg890 and Arg891 of yMtr4 point towards Asp86, Glu90, and Asp96 of yRrp6.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: Similar architectural features in the positioning of hMTR4 and hRRP6N-hRRP47 in the human complex were found, with the corresponding, conserved residues Arg856, Arg859 and Arg860 in hMTR4 and Asp118, Glu121 and Asp129 in hRRP6.
source: The finding of similar architectural features in the positioning of hMTR4 and hRRP6N-hRRP47 in the human complex (with the corresponding, conserved residues Arg856, Arg859 and Arg860 in hMTR4 and Asp118, Glu121 and Asp129 in hRRP6) prompted us to assess the importance of this conserved interaction in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Growth of the mtr4-RRR-EGFP strain (with R887E, R890E, R891E mutations in yMtr4) was severely affected.
source: Growth of the corresponding mtr4-RRR-EGFP strain was severely affected (Figure 7B), indicating that impairing the yRrp6N-yRrp47-binding surface of yMtr4 has deleterious effects in yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by the growth assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Impairing the yRrp6N-yRrp47-binding surface of yMtr4 has deleterious effects in yeast.
source: Growth of the corresponding mtr4-RRR-EGFP strain was severely affected (Figure 7B), indicating that impairing the yRrp6N-yRrp47-binding surface of yMtr4 has deleterious effects in yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the growth assay data.

claim: The conserved interaction between yMtr4 and the yRrp6N-yRrp47 module is important for function in vivo.
source: These results suggest that the conserved interaction between yMtr4 and the yRrp6N-yRrp47 module is important for function in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and growth assay data.

claim: The yeast and human nuclear exosome complexes share a similar overall structure and biochemical properties, forming macromolecular assemblies that effectively function as a cage to trap RNA substrates channeled to degradation.
source: The yeast and human nuclear exosome complexes indeed share a similar overall structure and biochemical properties, forming macromolecular assemblies that effectively function as a cage to trap RNA substrates channeled to degradation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the structural and biochemical comparisons.

claim: One change between the yeast and human exosome core complexes is the relative strength of the interaction between the 9-subunit scaffold and the exoribonuclease.
source: One such change between the yeast and human exosome core complexes is the relative strength of the interaction between the 9-subunit scaffold and the exoribonuclease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: In the case of the human complex, hDIS3 binds hEXO-9 at a similar position as the yeast complex, but with fewer interactions.
source: In the case of the human complex, hDIS3 binds hEXO-9 at a similar position as the yeast complex, but with fewer interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The weaker binding detected from the structural and biochemical data rationalizes why hDIS3 was not even identified as a component in earlier proteomic studies of endogenous exosome complexes and could only be detected with sensitive SILAC-based mass-spectrometry approaches.
source: The weaker binding that we detect from the structural and biochemical data rationalizes why hDIS3 was not even identified as a component in earlier proteomic studies of endogenous exosome complexes (Chen et al., 2001) and could only be detected with sensitive SILAC-based mass-spectrometry approaches (Tomecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation that connects the structural findings to previous proteomic studies.

claim: The modulation in the strength of the interaction may have functional consequences on the regulation of hEXO-10 assembly.
source: We speculate that the modulation in the strength of the interaction may have functional consequences on the regulation of hEXO-10 assembly.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications.

claim: In yeast, there is a single yRrp44 protein that is part of both the nuclear and cytoplasmic forms of the exosome.
source: In yeast, there is a single yRrp44 protein that is part of both the nuclear and cytoplasmic forms of the exosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the yeast exosome.

claim: The current view is that yeast yRrp44 assembles together with yExo-9 in the cytoplasm and is transported to the nucleus by the import capacity of yRrp6.
source: The current view is that yeast yRrp44 assembles together with yExo-9 in the cytoplasm and is transported to the nucleus by the import capacity of yRrp6 (Gonzales-Zubiate et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In human cells, there are two different paralogues (hDIS3 and hDIS3L) that have to be selectively incorporated in the nuclear and cytoplasmic forms of the complex.
source: Instead, the situation is more complex in human cells, as there are instead two different paralogues (hDIS3 and hDIS3L) that have to be selectively incorporated in the nuclear and cytoplasmic forms of the complex (Tomecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Bio-informatics analyses predict the presence of a possible NLS in the sequence of hDIS3, within a C-terminal part of the molecule (residues 949–958) that in the cryo-EM structure is accessibly exposed to the solvent.
source: It is unclear at the moment where the human nuclear exosome core is assembled, but we note that bio-informatics analyses predict the presence of a possible NLS in the sequence of hDIS3, within a C-terminal part of the molecule (residues 949–958) that in the cryo-EM structure is accessibly exposed to the solvent.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis and structural observation.

claim: A separate nuclear import of hDIS3, independent from that of hEXO-9-hRRP6-hRRP47, would allow the formation of the correct nuclear assembly, and a lower affinity of hDIS3 for hEXO-9 may be important in this context.
source: We speculate that a separate nuclear import of hDIS3, independent from that of hEXO-9-hRRP6-hRRP47, would allow the formation of the correct nuclear assembly, and a lower affinity of hDIS3 for hEXO-9 may be important in this context.
evidence: This is a speculation about the assembly mechanism.

claim: Another isoform of hDIS3 is translated from an mRNA with an alternative exon in the 5' coding region, resulting in a smaller PIN domain that might further impact on the binding affinity for hEXO-9 and/or the RNA binding properties.
source: As a note, another isoform of hDIS3 is translated from an mRNA with an alternative exon in the 5' coding region, resulting in a smaller PIN domain that might therefore further impact on the binding affinity for hEXO-9 and/or the RNA binding properties.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications of an alternative isoform.

claim: The exoribonuclease region of hDIS3 is more similar in terms of RNA path to bacterial RNase II and to human DIS3L2 than it is to its yeast orthologue yRrp44.
source: Unexpectedly when considering the levels of sequence conservation, the exoribonuclease region of hDIS3 is more similar in terms of RNA path to bacterial RNase II and to human DIS3L2 (a paralogue that functions independently of the exosome complex) than it is to its yeast orthologue yRrp44.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The difference in RNA path impacts on the RNA-channeling path in the exosome core.
source: The difference in turn impacts on the RNA-channeling path in the exosome core.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: In the yeast complex, Rrp44 can adopt either a closed conformation to support the RNA channel path or an open conformation to support a short direct path to the exoribonuclease site.
source: In the yeast complex, Rrp44 can adopt either a closed conformation to support the RNA channel path or an open conformation to support a short direct path to the exoribonuclease site (Makino et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In the human complex, the RNA channel path is achieved by an open conformation of hDIS3.
source: In the human complex, the RNA channel path is achieved by an open conformation of hDIS3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: None of the 2D or 3D particle classes obtained during processing of the cryo-EM dataset showed a density of hDIS3 corresponding to the closed yRrp44 conformation.
source: None of the 2D or 3D particle classes obtained during processing of the cryo-EM dataset showed a density of hDIS3 corresponding to the closed yRrp44 conformation.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The open conformation of hDIS3 could in principle also support the direct access route.
source: In principle, the open conformation of hDIS3 could also support the direct access route, but whether this may be favored for at least a subset of nuclear transcripts as in the case of yeast (Han and van Hoof, 2016) is currently unclear.
evidence: This is a speculation about possible alternative RNA paths.

claim: The channel path of hEXO-10 is used also in the context of hEXO-14 by RNA substrates that are unwound by hMTR4.
source: The channel path of hEXO-10 is used also in the context of hEXO-14 by RNA substrates that are unwound by hMTR4.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure of hEXO-14.

claim: hMTR4 is positioned on top of hEXO-10 with a similar edge-on conformation as previously observed in yeast.
source: This helicase is positioned on top of hEXO-10 with a similar edge-on conformation as previously observed in yeast (Schuller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure and citation to previous work.

claim: While this work was in revision, similar structural findings were reported.
source: We note that while this work was in revision, similar structural findings were reported (Weick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a note about concurrent work.
